name: Erik Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers stay confidential. Walk me through an ordinary working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Erik, 27, and I studied percussion through a master’s degree. I lead rhythm sessions for a small recording studio, play live dates and teach young drummers; a normal day moves between click tracks, microphones and a rehearsal room. I love a take where everyone finally locks together. I do not love sending three reminders before a studio pays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where do pay and security stand for you now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The pay is typical for a working musician, not spectacular. I live with my partner, who is studying, and I cover most of the rent; I have about four months of expenses saved. There are some other studio and teaching jobs nearby, but I would need to audition for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the studio that the tools are handy for sorting takes and writing cue lists, but we still need people to play. I'm happy to use one when it gives us more rehearsal time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Routine admin is a nuisance, so I wouldn't mourn it. My worry is still a late studio payment, not a machine taking my drum chair this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the studio sessions, six weekly pupils and live dates. Starting now I'd test a new AI cue-list tool on my own recordings, check every time stamp myself, and use it through the first year only if it saves an hour without exposing a pupil's file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm calm about the work, though I keep an eye on cash coming in. Four months of expenses means a late invoice is annoying instead of a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the saved time be worth to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An hour back lets me prepare an extra lesson or take a walk before the late show. It will not turn a low-fee recording day into a good one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you keep your pupils safe when you use a tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI every day for drafts, but I keep my pupils' audio off those services. I test with my own playing and check the output before a cue list reaches anyone else.

say: I would welcome **cue-list tools** that give musicians more rehearsal time.
I would still insist that **people** play the actual studio and live parts.
think: Late **studio payments** worry me more than small routine automation.
My **four-month cushion** makes delayed invoices irritating but manageable.
do: Keep six **weekly pupils**, studio sessions and live dates through the first year.
Test a new **AI cue-list tool** on my own recordings and check every time stamp.
Use the tool only if it **saves time** without exposing pupils’ files.
feel: I feel **calm** about paid work while watching delayed invoices.
S0.quote: Four months of expenses means a late invoice is annoying instead of a crisis.
fieldNote: His **daily AI use** includes drafts, but he excludes pupils’ audio from those services.
A **moderate cushion** and typical pay let him test tools without needing a quick income rescue.

steps.text: Keep six weekly pupils, studio sessions and live dates
Test new AI cue-list tool on own recordings and check time stamps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a cheap backing track can replace some studio calls, but a live band is still a shared job. I'd want the players to set licensing terms together instead of each taking a lower fee alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My short percussion overdubs would go first; a producer can ask a tool for ten versions. Losing two studio days a month would eat the money I put aside for our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd learn a new AI stem editor using only tracks I own, so I can show clients what a real player adds. In the first year, if overdub calls fall, I'd pitch a paid rhythm lab at the youth centre, but only if the centre funds the room and enough pupils enrol.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be anxious, not helpless. I can switch my offer toward teaching. An empty room doesn't pay me for being inventive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which paid job would disappear first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The smallest overdub day is often the first one a producer cancels. I would log those cancellations for three months before deciding whether my studio hours are actually shrinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask other studio musicians to do with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask studio players to agree on minimum session fees and permission before our tracks train a tool. A licence that follows the recording is worth more than one angry post online.

say: I would defend **live bands** while admitting that cheap tracks can replace some studio calls.
I would ask players to set shared **licensing terms** before accepting lower fees.
think: Short **percussion overdubs** could be replaced before my live dates disappear.
Losing two **studio days** monthly would reduce the money reserved for rent.
do: Learn a new **AI stem editor** this month using only tracks I own.
Pitch a paid **rhythm lab** if overdubs fall and the centre funds a room with enough enrolment.
Seek **minimum session fees** and recording permission with studio players.
feel: I feel **anxious** about fewer studio calls, though I can test teaching.
S1.quote: An empty room doesn't pay me for being inventive.
fieldNote: He names **overdub cancellations** as the first measurable loss and will log them for three months.
His **teaching trial** depends on funded room space and enough paying pupils.

steps.text: Learn new AI stem editor using only tracks he owns

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends that AGI could do almost all thinking work by 2028, including arranging and choosing sounds. A robot that plays as well as us is the later 2031 problem, so those are separate shocks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio could stop buying my arrangement notes and many overdubs before anyone builds a good robot drummer. I pay most of our rent, and four months of savings would run down fast if half the sessions vanished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I'd separate my live, lesson and studio earnings on paper, and save an extra share of every session fee. In the first year after AGI arrives, if studio bookings halve, I'd cut paid rehearsal space, offer the youth centre lab if it funds the room, and apply for an open school percussion post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be alarmed by the speed of the pay loss. I can try a new class, but two years is barely enough to learn whether parents will pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do before 2028, and what happens after?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A live set might still book me before 2031, but it happens twice a month, not five days a week. The three years before capable robots arrive don't cover the thinking work the studio buys from me now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the live set really protect your income until 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner exactly when the savings would run out at half my normal studio pay. We would pause our holiday deposit first, not wait until rent was due.

say: I would separate **2028 AGI** for thinking tasks from capable robots around 2031.
I would explain that **arrangements** may disappear before hands-on playing does.
think: The studio could stop buying my **notes and overdubs** quickly.
Our **rent** relies mostly on me, and savings could erode if half the sessions vanish.
do: Separate **earnings** from live work, lessons and studio sessions now, then save extra session fees.
Cut paid **rehearsal space** if bookings halve after 2028.
Apply for an open **school percussion post** if studio income collapses.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a possible fast loss of studio pay.
S2.quote: The three years before capable robots arrive don't cover the thinking work the studio buys from me now.
fieldNote: He sees the **2028 thinking shock** hitting paid studio work before robots can play in 2031.
His **fallbacks** require lost bookings, a funded youth-centre room and an actual school opening.

steps.text: Save extra share of each studio session fee before 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the studio team that five years is enough to make new agreements, if we actually start. Thinking AGI arrives around 2031 in this picture, and capable robots come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could turn my rhythm lab into a regular class before the studio work is under pressure. I still need paid enrolments, and I won't hand a venue the rights to a whole group performance for a single rehearsal fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I'd run two paid trial classes at the youth centre if it funds a room and six learners register. Before 2031 I'd help studio players draft a shared recording licence; in the first year after AGI arrives, I'd expand the class only if it covers my teaching time and ask the school about any open post if studio hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy, but I have a test I can measure. The five-year stretch lets me change the mix of work without cancelling good sessions on a forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test during the five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six learners at the posted fee would cover two hours of teaching and bus fare. If only three enrol, I would cancel the second date rather than quietly spend our rent on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know whether a cooperative session is paying its way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The licence must say when a recording can be reused and how each player is paid. If we cannot agree that among ourselves, the studio will keep negotiating with us one at a time.

say: I would push for **shared recording licences** before thinking AGI arrives around 2031.
I would remind players that capable **robots** follow around 2034.
think: A regular **rhythm class** could replace some lost studio money if pupils pay.
One rehearsal fee should not buy a venue the **rights** to a whole group performance.
do: Run two paid **trial classes** if the youth centre funds a room and six learners register.
Draft a shared **recording licence** with studio players before 2031.
Expand classes after 2031 only if fees cover my **teaching time**.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, with enough time to measure a class before changing work.
S3.quote: The five-year stretch lets me change the mix of work without cancelling good sessions on a forecast.
fieldNote: He uses a **six-learner threshold** and cancels the second date if only three enrol.
He wants a **licence** stating reuse terms and each musician’s pay before recordings spread.

steps.text: Run paid youth-centre trials if room is funded and six learners register

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger players that a decade is time to make a teaching room and a live audience, while keeping our recordings under fair terms. Thinking AGI comes in 2036 and player-level robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be 37 when the studio's thinking tasks change and 40 when the hands-on machines arrive. I don't assume drums become safe forever just because an audience likes people now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep my six pupils and studio dates and save part of each session fee. Over the decade I'd build the rhythm lab only when paid enrolments cover the room; in the first year after 2036 I'd keep classes and live gigs that still pay, then look for a school vacancy if the studio contracts end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cautiously secure because I can test several classes before making a big move. Our rent still relies mostly on me, so I won't spend the cushion on equipment just because the future sounds exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a decade let you build that two years could not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years lets a shy first class grow by word of mouth and gives me time to qualify for school teaching if the work requires it. I would pay for the qualification only after checking a real vacancy's requirements and whether my class income covers tuition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner about the rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show my partner the class receipts and the studio bookings every quarter. I won't buy a new drum kit out of our rent fund to prove I can adapt.

I would place **2036 thinking AGI** before capable robots around 2039.

feel: I feel cautiously **secure**, while refusing to spend rent money on speculative equipment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the studio might lose half its paid work before a new class is ready. A funded youth-centre room and a short income bridge tied to cancelled session dates would help. Shared licensing rules would also stop each player from being pushed into a private bargain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who bears the cost when musicians are told to experiment. A studio can call a new tool exciting while I pay the bus fare, the room deposit and the missed session fee.

headlineQuote: A studio can call a new tool exciting while I pay the bus fare, the room deposit and the missed session fee.
portrait: Erik is a **27-year-old percussionist** with a master’s degree who leads studio sessions, teaches six pupils and plays live dates.
His **typical pay** and four-month cushion support experiments, although he covers most of the rent with a studying partner.
He uses **AI daily** but tests new tools on owned tracks and keeps pupils’ recordings off services.
Fast AGI threatens **studio overdubs** before robots can play; he tests a funded rhythm lab and pursues shared licences.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** could halve paid studio work before a rhythm class earns enough.
whatWouldHelp: A funded **youth-centre room** and short income bridge would let him test the class after lost sessions.
Shared **licensing rules** would protect players from individual pressure over recording reuse.
